summary: Defines Traversal Using Relays around NAT, a protocol that lets a host behind a NAT use a relay server to exchange packets with peers when direct communication is impossible. A client can talk to multiple peers using a single relay address. It was designed as part of the Interactive Connectivity Establishment approach. It replaces RFC 5766.

plainLanguage.summary: This protocol lets a computer hidden behind a router send and receive data through a middle server on the public Internet. The computer asks the server for an address of its own, and the server forwards traffic between that address and the computers it wants to reach.

subtitle: Lets a host behind a NAT reach a peer through a relay server, using one relayed address for many peers.

tldr.problem: A host behind a NAT often cannot open a direct path to another host behind a NAT, and the usual trick of punching a hole through both NATs fails when both of them map addresses in a restrictive way.
tldr.mechanism: TURN lets the client ask a relay server for a relayed transport address. The client authenticates itself, keeps the allocation alive with a Refresh request, installs a permission for each peer it wants to talk to, and then sends data to the server either in a Send indication or in a ChannelData message.
tldr.outcome: One relayed address can serve many peers at once, which distinguishes TURN from other relay protocols, and the permission mechanism keeps enterprise firewalls happy. The relay costs bandwidth, so it should be used only when no direct path can be found.

today: RFC 8656 is a Proposed Standard published in February 2020. It obsoletes RFC 5766 and RFC 6156, and the unit metadata lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why a Relay Is Sometimes Needed
sections.content:
A host behind a NAT may wish to exchange packets with other hosts, some of which may also be behind NATs. The hosts can use hole punching techniques to try to discover a direct communication path, that is, a path from one host to another through the intervening NATs and routers that does not traverse any relays. As described in RFC 5128 and RFC 4787, hole punching fails if both hosts are behind NATs that are not well behaved, for example when both NATs have a mapping behaviour of address-dependent mapping or address-and-port-dependent mapping.

When a direct path cannot be found, it is necessary to use the services of an intermediate host that acts as a relay for the packets, typically sitting in the public Internet.

In many enterprise networks, direct UDP transmissions are not permitted between clients on internal networks and external IP addresses. To permit media sessions to use UDP and avoid forcing them through TCP, an enterprise firewall can be configured to allow UDP traffic relayed through an enterprise relay server, and WebRTC requires support for this scenario. Some users of SIP or WebRTC want IP location privacy from the remote peer, and can select a relay server offering it, conveying only the relayed candidates to the peer for ICE connectivity checks.

TURN allows a host behind a NAT, the TURN client, to ask another host, the TURN server, to act as a relay. The client arranges for the server to relay packets to and from certain other hosts, the peers, and controls aspects of how the relaying is done by obtaining an IP address and port on the server, the relayed transport address. When a peer sends a packet to that address, the server relays the transport protocol data to the client inside a message header that says which peer it came from. When the client sends a message to the server, the server identifies the remote peer from the message header and relays the data to the intended peer.

TURN differs from other relay control protocols in that it allows a client to communicate with multiple peers using a single relay address. It was designed as one piece in the larger ICE approach to NAT traversal, but it can also be used without ICE. It is an extension to the STUN protocol, and most, though not all, TURN messages are STUN-formatted.
sections.plainLanguage: Two machines behind two routers often cannot reach each other directly, because each router only lets its own machine talk to the outside. A relay in the middle sends the traffic for them, and this protocol is the rules for that relay.

sections.title: The Words the Protocol Uses
sections.content:
The protocol is an extension to STUN, and the reader is expected to be familiar with RFC 8489 and its terms. The terms this document adds are precise.

A transport address is the combination of an IP address and a port. A host transport address is a transport address on a client or a peer. A server-reflexive transport address is a transport address on the external side of a NAT, allocated by the NAT to correspond to a specific host transport address. A relayed transport address is a transport address on the TURN server used for relaying packets between the client and a peer. The TURN server transport address is the address the client uses to send TURN messages to the server, and the peer transport address is the address of the peer as the server sees it, which is the peer's server-reflexive address when the peer is behind a NAT.

An allocation is the relayed transport address granted to a client through an Allocate request, along with related state such as permissions and expiration timers. A permission is the IP address and transport protocol, but not the port, of a peer that is permitted to send traffic to the server and have it relayed to the client. A channel is a channel number and associated peer transport address, used for the more bandwidth-efficient ChannelData message. A realm is a string describing the server or a context within it, and it tells the client which username and password combination to use. A nonce is a string chosen at random by the server and included in its response; to prevent replay attacks the server should change it regularly.

The 5-tuple is the combination of client IP address and port, server IP address and port, and transport protocol, and it uniquely identifies the communication stream and the allocation on the server.
sections.plainLanguage: Each address in this protocol has a specific name. The important distinction is between the address the computer itself has, the address the NAT gives it on the outside, and the address the relay server hands out on the Internet.

sections.title: How a Session Is Set Up
sections.content:
The client sends TURN messages from its host transport address to the TURN server transport address, which it learns by some unspecified means such as configuration, and which is typically used by many clients at once. Because the client is behind a NAT, the server sees its packets as coming from the client's server-reflexive transport address, and packets sent there by the server reach the client's host transport address through the NAT.

The client uses TURN commands to create and manipulate an allocation on the server, a data structure that contains the relayed transport address and is uniquely identified by it. Once an allocation exists, the client can send application data to the server along with an indication of which peer it is for, and the server relays it to that peer in a UDP datagram using the relayed address as the source. In the reverse direction, a peer sends a UDP datagram to the relayed transport address, the server encapsulates the data inside a TURN message and sends it to the client along with an indication of which peer sent it. Because every message says which peer it concerns, one allocation can serve many peers. When the peer is behind a NAT, the client must identify it by its server-reflexive transport address rather than its host transport address.

Between the server and the peer, TURN always uses UDP. Between the client and the server, the specification allows UDP, TCP, TLS over TCP or DTLS over UDP. (D)TLS is supported because it gives the client a way to confirm it is talking to the correct server and keeps the control messages confidential, but TURN does not require it because the overhead is higher than that of digest authentication, and most application data would end up encrypted twice.

This version of TURN is designed so that the server can be implemented as an application running in user space without special privileges, which makes it easy to deploy. The consequences are that the Diffserv field may not be preserved across the server, the Time to Live field may be reset rather than decremented, the ECN field may be reset, and there is no end-to-end fragmentation because the packet is reassembled at the server.
sections.plainLanguage: The client asks the server for an address, and the server gives it one. Everything the client sends goes to that address, and everything the peers send there is passed on to the client with a note of which peer it was.

sections.title: Allocations and Permissions
sections.content:
To create an allocation the client sends an Allocate request and the server replies with an Allocate success response containing the allocated relayed transport address. The client can include attributes describing the type of allocation it desires, such as its lifetime. Since relaying data has security implications, the server requires the client to authenticate itself, typically using STUN's long-term credential mechanism or the STUN Extension for Third-Party Authorization, to show that it is authorized to use the server. A request with missing or invalid credentials is rejected with a 401 error, and the client repeats the request with credentials.

Once a relayed transport address is allocated the client must keep the allocation alive by periodically sending a Refresh request. TURN deliberately uses a different method for refreshes, rather than a new Allocate request, to ensure that the client is informed if the allocation vanishes for some reason. The default lifetime of an allocation is 10 minutes, chosen to be long enough that refreshing is not typically a burden while expiring allocations whose client has unexpectedly quit. The client can request a longer lifetime and may modify the request in a Refresh request, and the server always states the actual lifetime in the response. The client must issue a new Refresh transaction within the lifetime seconds of the previous Allocate or Refresh transaction, and it deletes the allocation by sending a Refresh request with a requested lifetime of zero.

Both the server and the client keep track of the 5-tuple used in the Allocate request, and subsequent messages use the same one, so both know which allocation is meant. A second relayed transport address requires a second allocation using a different 5-tuple.

TURN includes the notion of permissions to ease the concerns of enterprise administrators that TURN could be used to bypass corporate firewall security; permissions mimic the address-restricted filtering mechanism of NATs that comply with RFC 4787. An allocation can have zero or more permissions, each consisting of an IP address and a lifetime. When the server receives a UDP datagram on the relayed transport address it first checks the permissions, and relays the data only if the source IP address matches a permission, otherwise it silently discards the datagram. A permission expires after 5 minutes if it is not refreshed, and there is no way to explicitly delete one. The client installs or refreshes a permission with a CreatePermission request or a ChannelBind request, and for security reasons permissions can only be installed by transactions that can be authenticated, so Send indications and ChannelData messages install none.
sections.plainLanguage: The client proves who it is, then keeps the arrangement alive with a periodic refresh. It also has to name each peer it wants to hear from, and that permission lapses after five minutes unless it is renewed.

sections.title: Sending Data: Indications
sections.content:
There are two mechanisms for exchanging application data. The first uses the Send and Data methods, the second uses channels. Both let the client talk to several peers over a single relayed transport address, and both include a way for the client to say which peer the data is for and for the server to say which peer the data came from.

The client sends a Send indication containing an XOR-PEER-ADDRESS attribute with the server-reflexive transport address of the peer and a DATA attribute holding the application data. The server extracts the data and sends it in a UDP datagram to the peer, using the allocated relay address as the source address; there is no need to specify the relayed transport address, since it is implied by the 5-tuple used for the Send indication. In the reverse direction, UDP datagrams arriving at the relayed transport address are converted into Data indications and sent to the client, with the peer's server-reflexive transport address in an XOR-PEER-ADDRESS attribute and the data in a DATA attribute. Some ICMP packets arriving at the relayed transport address may also be converted into Data indications, with the ICMP type and code in an ICMP attribute.

Send and Data indications cannot be authenticated, because the long-term credential mechanism of STUN does not support authenticating indications. This is less serious than it first appears, because the client-to-server leg is only half of the total path to the peer; applications that want end-to-end security should encrypt the data between the client and the peer. Because Send indications are not authenticated, an attacker can send bogus ones to the server, which will then relay them to a peer, so TURN requires the client to install a permission towards a peer before sending data to it with a Send indication.
sections.plainLanguage: To send to a peer, the client puts the data and the peer's address in one message to the server. The server pulls the data out and sends it as an ordinary datagram to the peer.

sections.title: Sending Data: Channels, Methods and Attributes
sections.content:
For some applications such as voice over IP, the 36 bytes of overhead that a Send or Data indication adds to the application data can substantially increase the bandwidth needed between the client and the server. The second mechanism uses the ChannelData message, which does not use the STUN header but has a 4-byte header holding a channel number and a length. Each channel number in use is bound to a specific peer, so it is a shorthand for that peer's address.

To bind a channel the client sends a ChannelBind request with an unbound channel number and the transport address of the peer. The client can then send data in ChannelData messages, and the server relays data from that peer back in a ChannelData message. Channel bindings last 10 minutes unless refreshed, a lifetime chosen to be longer than the permission lifetime, and unlike allocations there is no way to explicitly delete a binding. Once a channel is bound the client may still use a Send indication, for example to use the DONT-FRAGMENT attribute, but the server must use the ChannelData message whenever a channel has been bound to the peer.

The STUN methods defined are Allocate with code 0x003, Refresh 0x004, Send 0x006, Data 0x007, CreatePermission 0x008 and ChannelBind 0x009. The attributes include CHANNEL-NUMBER 0x000C, LIFETIME 0x000D, XOR-PEER-ADDRESS 0x0012, DATA 0x0013, XOR-RELAYED-ADDRESS 0x0016, REQUESTED-ADDRESS-FAMILY 0x0017, EVEN-PORT 0x0018, REQUESTED-TRANSPORT 0x0019, DONT-FRAGMENT 0x001A, RESERVATION-TOKEN 0x0022, ADDITIONAL-ADDRESS-FAMILY 0x8000, ADDRESS-ERROR-CODE 0x8001 and ICMP 0x8004. The DONT-FRAGMENT attribute asks the server to set the DF bit in the IP header when relaying the data onward, and has no value part.
sections.plainLanguage: Once a peer has been given a short number, the client can use a four-byte header instead of a full message, which saves bandwidth on a busy link.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Most of the attacks on TURN are mitigated by the server requiring requests to be authenticated, and this specification requires the use of authentication. The mandatory-to-implement mechanism is the long-term credential mechanism of STUN; other mechanisms of equal or stronger security properties may be used if they can be invoked in an interoperable way.

Among the outsider attacks, obtaining unauthorized allocations is prevented by the long-term credential mechanism, which lets the server determine the identity of the requestor and whether it is allowed to obtain the allocation. The offline dictionary attack is mitigated by using a nonce that the server changes regularly. Faked refreshes and permissions are handled by the authentication of those transactions. Fake data is the reason for the requirement that a permission must exist before a Send indication is relayed. Impersonating a server is prevented by the realm and nonce mechanism, and by the option of using (D)TLS to confirm the server's identity. Eavesdropping traffic is a matter for the application to protect with its own encryption, since TURN does not encrypt the relayed data. The TURN loop attack, in which a peer sends data to itself, is mitigated by the requirement that the relayed transport address must be used as the source address of relayed traffic.

Insider attacks include denial of service against the TURN server, anonymous relaying of malicious traffic, and manipulating other allocations. A separate concern is the tunnel amplification attack, in which an attacker causes packets to loop between a TURN server and a tunnel between IPv4 and IPv6 until the TURN headers are used up. The amplification potential is limited by the MTU, so IPv6 with UDP and TURN takes 334 bytes and a four-to-one amplification out of a 1500-byte packet is possible. The attack is mitigated by the recommendation that TURN servers not accept allocation or channel-binding requests from addresses known to be tunnelled and not forward data to such addresses, and a server must not accept Teredo or 6to4 addresses in these requests.
sections.plainLanguage: The server checks who is asking before it does anything, and it refuses to relay to addresses that are known tunnels, because that is how a packet can be made to circle forever.

sections.title: What Changed From the Earlier Versions
sections.content:
The major changes in the TURN protocol from the original RFC 5766 specification are IPv6 support, the REQUESTED-ADDRESS-FAMILY attribute, a description of the tunnel amplification attack, DTLS support, support for receiving ICMP packets, updates to Path MTU Discovery, discovery of the TURN server, the TURN URI scheme semantics, Happy Eyeballs for TURN, and alignment with the changes in STUN of RFC 8489.

The major updates to RFC 6156, which had added IPv6 support, are the ADDITIONAL-ADDRESS-FAMILY and ADDRESS-ERROR-CODE attributes, 440 (Address Family not Supported) and 443 (Peer Address Family Mismatch) responses, more detail on packet translation, and TCP-to-UDP and UDP-to-TCP relaying.
sections.plainLanguage: The new version adds IPv6, a way to find the server, DTLS support, and a description of an attack that the older version did not cover.
